title: Natural Resources Police use thermal imaging to rescue lost kayaker in Talbot County
author: Konner Metz
content:
Natural Resources Police use thermal imaging to rescue lost kayaker in Talbot County

 July 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 344
 Words 

 Read News Document

 BROAD CREEK — Police and firefighters teamed to locate a lost juvenile kayaker last weekend in Talbot County.On July 4 around 10 p.m., Maryland Natural Resources Police were informed of a lost kayaker in the Broad Creek area, which is on the west side of the county south of St. Michaels. Officials said he was on the water for "several hours" and around three miles from home.
Using thermal imaging cameras, a Natural Resource Police aviation unit quickly found the lost person — in around five minutes, according to Sgt. John Buchanan, chief pilot for NRP. Buchanan was in the aircraft with tactical flight officer Christian Helwig.
Buchanan said the kayaker left out of Grace Creek.
"I think it got dark on him, and he didn't know where he was," Buchanan said.
Once located, police used a spotlight to direct a rescue boat from the Tilghman Island Volunteer Fire Company toward the juvenile.
A video posted to Facebook by Natural Resource Police shows the aircraft hone in on the kayaker and direct the fire boat to retrieve the juvenile.
Buchanan said such a rescue isn't too common, but it become somewhat prominent during boating season.
"(The) Chesapeake Bay and the tributaries are very large," Buchanan said. "When you start thinking about the different rivers and creeks and stuff off the Chesapeake Bay, we go out on different search missions like that probably a few times a month."
The pilot emphasized Helwig's expertise is crucial to such rescues. Helwig handles the thermal imaging camera, which can expose subjects in dark conditions, as well as a mapping system to pull up addresses and latitudes and longitudes.
"He's gotten really good with it, he's worked really hard at it," Buchanan said. "He's made us as a team very successful going out and doing these search missions."
Buchanan advises those going out on the water, especially alone, to be prepared with a charged cell phone and other equipment in case of emergency.
"Have a life jacket if you're out at night," he said. "Obviously have some kind of flashlight. And know the area, that's probably the biggest thing."

Construction advances for first responder training campus

 May 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News

 EASTON — Construction on the A. James Clark Emergency Services Training Campus is well underway — and project leaders even had the chance to show Gov. Wes Moore around the construction site last week.Brett Whitehead, president of Friends of the Easton Volunteer Fire Department, has spearheaded fundraising efforts for the state-of-the-art training campus, which will be used by firefighters, police officers and EMS workers when it opens.
Whitehead said construction teams have made "unbelievable progress."
The 7,200-square-foot campus is located on Mistletoe Drive. Once complete, Easton Volunteer Fire Department Assistant Chief Daryl Caldwell said it will include a 4,200-square-foot classroom building, a burn building for search-and-rescue and active shooter simulations, and two pads for car fire and extrication training.
The burn building won't be damaged, project leaders say, since it's going to be a metal building with concrete floors and stairs. It will have movable walls to provide a variety of room configurations during trainings.
Caldwell said the training campus will keep on-duty first responders centrally located. The campus also will reduce long travel times that local first responders often incur when going to Salisbury or the western shore for necessary training.
Ground was broken in December on the project. As of Monday, significant work had been done to both the classroom and burn buildings. Whitehead said the goal of opening by the end of the year still remains.
"If weather holds up, permits get approved," he said.
Whitehead said more than $4 million has been raised, which leaves less than $1 million remaining of the project's $5 million fundraising goal.
As the name indicates, the A. James & Alice B. Clark Foundation was fundamental in fundraising efforts. Last September, the foundation donated $1 million to the training campus. Overall, the foundation has contributed $1.9 million to the project.
The project also has received $300,000 in state grant funding.
On April 29, Moore toured the training campus as part of a private visit in Easton.
Caldwell said Moore was "very attentive" and asked many questions. Caldwell, Whitehead and other members of the department, along with town leaders, were present for the governor's visit.
"Governor Moore's visit to the A. James Clark Emergency Services Training Campus site in Easton highlights his continued commitment to public safety, and ensuring Maryland is providing our law enforcement and first responder personnel with the best resources available," Moore's office said in a statement. "The governor is proud to work alongside so many local electeds and community leaders in supporting this project."
Whitehead believes the Easton training campus will be a model for future first responder training facilities where personnel can train separately or together.
"This is the only one of its kind in the Mid-Shore period," Whitehead said. "Where you have real-time training opportunities. You have all first responders training together. No other site does that in the Mid-Shore."

title: Mid-Shore could see highs in upper 90s as heat wave approaches
author: Konner Metz

Mid-Shore could see highs in upper 90s as heat wave approaches

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News

 EASTON — As many regions in the United States prepare for a significant heat wave in the coming days, Maryland's Mid-Shore could see temperatures nearing triple digits next week.According to the National Weather Service, Easton is projected to see highs around 95 to 97 degrees beginning Sunday through Wednesday. Highs are expected to remain in the 90s later in the week across Caroline, Dorchester and Talbot counties.
The Dorchester County Health Department is encouraging people stay out of the sun when temperatures peak in the late mornings and early afternoons.
A press release from the department noted the following groups should take added precautions: babies, young children, pregnant women, older adults, outside workers and those without air conditioning.
Local health officials recommend regularly hydrating, limiting time outdoors and monitoring for signs of heat exhaustion — heavy sweating, cold skin, cramps, dizziness, nausea or vomiting, etc.
The Maryland Department of Health said in a press release this week that Maryland saw 26 heat-related deaths last year. The state department added that parents and guardians should never leave children in cars.
"Remember to check on those who are particularly vulnerable to heat, including young children, senior citizens, and people with chronic diseases — and confirm that they have the resources they need to stay safe during the hottest months," said Maryland Secretary of Health Dr. Meena Seshamani in the release.
EASTON FIRE PREPARES
As temperatures heat up, volunteer fire departments across the Mid-Shore remain on call. Due to the physically intensive work of firefighting and the heavy gear that must be worn, some departments are asking for water donations from the community.
Easton Volunteer Fire Department Chief J.R. Dobson says his department has received enough cases of water from thoughtful community residents and businesses to get through next week's heat wave. Dobson is encouraging residents to contribute to other fire departments in need in Talbot County.
Whether it's lending bottled waters or assisting with manpower on a call, Dobson says local fire departments work together well.
"The other fire chiefs talk a lot, and we're always here to help one another," Dobson said.
The fire chief noted that as farmers in the area start to cut their wheat, field fires could pop up, a risk fire officials are keeping their eyes on.
Weather projections are accurate as of Friday afternoon.

title: Moms of children with special needs find respite at Hummingbird Inn
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Moms of children with special needs find respite at Hummingbird Inn

 January 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 1736
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Though the situations that brought six mothers of children with special needs to the Hummingbird Inn on a snowy January weekend are different, they shared a common thread: a desire to seek respite and connection.The weekend retreat, organized through nonprofit A Mother's Rest and held for the first time at the cozy Queen Anne Victorian bed and breakfast inn in Easton, provided the women with a much-needed and long-awaited chance to relax and refresh.
But the three-day weekend trip offered more than just respite — it gave the six mothers a space to be open and vulnerable with themselves and each other.
A Mother's RestFounded in 2017 by Andrea Roberts, A Mother's Rest Charitable Respite Foundation aims to improve the emotional and physical health of caregivers through affordable three-day weekend retreats.
The nonprofit operates two of its own respite inns — one in New Market, Maryland, and a second in northeastern Georgia. Both inns, open year-round, offer a multitude of weekend retreats for a variety of caregivers.
Bed and breakfast inns, like the Hummingbird, can participate, too, through A Mother's Rest's Porch Partners program, a national network of inns offering space for those seeking a break.
Eric Levinson, the owner and innkeeper at the Hummingbird Inn, learned about A Mother's Rest from his sister, a realtor in western Maryland who met Roberts.
Levinson reached out to Roberts, and from there, it became evident that his inn would be an ideal location for a respite retreat, he said.
There was also a personal connection for Levinson: his mother had specialized in working with children with disabilities and those in need of extra care, making the concept resonate even more.
"Just knowing other people who have these types of children or (who are) caretakers, and how much they give to them and take little for themselves … that opportunity just seemed like a really great thing to be able to do," he said.
Levinson first spoke with Roberts last January, blocking out all of his inn's rooms for the weekend. The inn was fully booked within three to four days, he said, meaning that the six women who came to Easton had been waiting for a year before coming to stay.
Though it's in the name, the nonprofit's retreats aren't just limited to mothers of children with special needs. The weekend trips are also offered for couples, dads, adoptive or foster parents, families and other caregivers in need of a break.
Some retreats are designated for caregivers dealing with specific disabilities or situations, like parents of children with Down syndrome or caregivers to combat-injured veterans.
But at each retreat, no matter the life circumstances that brought them there, the need for a weekend away to sleep and relax, and to have the opportunity to connect with others who understand their daily challenges, unites caregivers across all spectrums.
A weekend in EastonAlthough a snowstorm blanketed the Mid-Atlantic region on Friday, Jan. 19, it didn't deter six women from driving several hours to Easton for a weekend to themselves.
Check-in started at 3 p.m. on Friday, with inn staff helping each woman get settled in her room.
Each room, named after a town on the Eastern Shore, held a surprise care package with soaps, socks and eye masks. A floral arrangement also sat in each room, homed in a mug labeled "hug in a mug."
Though respite retreats affiliated with A Mother's Rest don't have planned activities, a number of local businesses that heard about the event reached out to Levinson asking how they could help to make the weekend even more special.
Out of the Fire offered a $50 credit for a meal. Legal Assets reached out with a special meal discount. Bluepoint Hospitality offered free coffee or beverages and free pastries, pie or ice cream. Friends called Levinson saying they'd like to buy the women a bottle of wine.
The community offered more than just food and drink, though — Chatterbox Hair Salon provided free shampoos, styles and blowouts, and the Avalon Theatre offered tickets to its weekend comedy or blues show.
Levinson and his team helped make reservations for the offerings and even drove some women to their hair appointments, taking away the stress of coordination.
"When I would talk to people about it, it was always the same: they knew somebody or they had a family member in this situation, and people just know how it's a lot, and you give up a lot — not begrudgingly, these are your family and children obviously, but everybody needs a break," Levinson said.
For Maureen Robinette, a mom from northern Delaware, the weekend served as a much-needed break from the busyness of raising her two active sons and her 9-year-old daughter with special needs.
"My husband will take my boys to whatever sporting event, he coaches them, he takes them to practices," she said. "So just every night, I'm on (daughter) duty, and it's just exhausting."
Robinette, who works full-time, spent her weekend walking around town, shopping, reading and enjoying breakfasts and dinners. She also took advantage of the offer from the nearby salon.
"It was amazing," she said of her experience, laughing. "It was very relaxing, I just felt we were pampered by this place.
And of course, as with any bed and breakfast, a mouthwatering meal was served every morning.
On Saturday, Levinson served up a sausage quiche and Belgian waffles. Sunday's menu boasted a blueberry yogurt parfait, a savory breakfast galette and creme brulee French toast.
And just before the women checked out on Monday, Levinson offered an Austrian egg cake, filled with leeks, eggs, cheese, onions and breadcrumbs, and pikelets, fluffy Australian pancakes topped with strawberry sauce.
Reflections and connectionsWhile the respite weekend primarily served as an opportunity to rest, with no pressure to do activities or engage with others, the six women who came to Easton found connections.
Over breakfast on Monday, Jan. 22, five mothers who stayed for the full weekend shared stories of hardships, interspersed with smiles at happy memories and positive developments with their children.
Candy Warner, a mom of two adult children, including a 30-year-old son who experiences uncontrollable seizures and aggression following a stroke before birth, traveled from near York, Pennsylvania, for the weekend retreat.
"It was wonderful, they always are," she said. "I'm always anxious to go home, but I don't want to go home because it's like reality."
Warner took the chance to connect with two of the other moms in Easton for the weekend, walking over to dinner at Scossa and talking in a candid way that only others like her could understand.
"I mean, we all have the same emotions, anywhere from being happy to being totally angry and frustrated, just on different levels depending on our children's diagnoses," she said. "So we can all relate to each other, no matter what diagnoses our children have or what we're going through."
"Sometimes there's a connection … you just feel like you just make a new friend for life," Warner added, choking up with emotion.
Robinette said it's easier to talk with other moms who are going through the same things, others who aren't going to judge or give unsolicited advice.
"I feel like all of us are here to just listen to our stories," she said, adding: "I just feel like it's just great to talk openly and share experiences, and understand what everyone else is going through, like stuff that you can't talk to your normal friends about."
Talking with normal friends can result in a look of pity, Warner said.
"I don't want your pity, just sit and listen to me sometimes," she said. "I don't need your feedback."
Robinette agreed.
"I didn't tell people at work for the longest time, because I just didn't want to get emotional, you don't want pity," she said with emotion in her voice. "Now I'm fairly open with it, because it's been long enough and it's just easier to explain stuff."
It can be isolating to parent a child with disabilities, said Melissa Egan Kerr, a mom of two from the Lehigh Valley in Pennsylvania. She said that feeling was compounded by the pandemic. And though some moms do choose to use the respite retreats to keep to themselves, the one in Easton was a little different.
"...This one, it is just like a really organic feeling of connecting with people and talking, and how therapeutic that is to just share your story with people who you know get what you're talking about," she said.
Deborah Adams, an adoptive mom of two children with trauma from earlier on in life, said A Mother's Rest retreats have saved her family, and at times, their sanity.
"It's easy to just feel so isolated … to just cut ourselves off," the Richmond, Virginia, mom said of her and her husband's experience raising their children with hidden disabilities. "And this is a way to get out of it and to have kind of some self-safety, and that's huge."
Adams found out about A Mother's Rest about four years ago, just before the COVID-19 pandemic.
"I went on a retreat, a random retreat," she said, "And all of the moms that were there, we all just connected on a level that you cannot connect with anyone."
A lasting impactEven before all of the women had checked in to the Hummingbird Inn that Friday afternoon, Levinson said he planned to host more respite retreats — a sentiment that still held true Monday morning at checkout.
"You could hear the gratitude in their voice, how much this meant to them," Levinson said of his six guests.
The weekend also held special meaning to Michael Abbott, the inn's event coordinator. Abbott, who lost his own mother at a young age, said he knew the retreat was something he wanted to give extra special care to.
For Abbott, that meant remembering the little things, like driving some of the mothers to their hair appointments or remembering that one guest preferred iced tea over coffee in the morning.
Being able to provide a safe, peaceful and welcoming space to decompress was meaningful to Abbott, too. He recalled one mother taking her first look at her room for the weekend.
"She's like, 'Oh my god, this is so lovely and so peaceful. I can see myself sitting here and reading in the corners. It's just what I need, and so inviting,'" he remembered.
To Abbott, that was clear.
"I just thought that she was ready to just let go, have a moment to herself, which I don't think she gets a lot," he said.
"It's just something they needed," Abbott added, choking up. "Moms go through a lot."

title: Talbot County's oldest firehouse is raising funds for reconstruction
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Talbot County's oldest firehouse is raising funds for reconstruction

 July 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 572

 TRAPPE — The oldest firehouse in Talbot County, the Trappe Volunteer Fire Company, is raising funds for much-needed reconstruction.Nick Newnam, chief of the Trappe Volunteer Fire Company described the building's structure as "questionable at best."
According to Newnam, the current firehouse structure dates from 1951 and no longer serves the needs of a modern fire company. The building's engine bay doors only provide "inches" of clearance, requiring custom sizing for new equipment. Structurally, the engine bay doors could not be expanded to accommodate larger fire vehicles.
About a year ago, the company began planning to fix the firehouse's problems. The estimated cost for the reconstruction, house fire equipment, training facilities, administrative space and housing quarters for a Talbot County Emergency Services Advanced Life Support unit would be $6 million, they discovered.
John Foster, president of the Trappe Volunteer Fire Company, said the company's leaders have contacted federal officials for assistance in the next budget cycle and have committed to raising 25% as matching funds.
The company's leaders are launching a "Raise a New Firehouse" fundraising campaign this summer, with a goal of $1.5 million over the next year.
The company set aside $450,000 to help accomplish the goal and is appealing to the community for help raising the remaining $1.05 million.
Along with the campaign, the company is seeking assistance from the community in developing fundraising efforts to achieve the annual goal.
"Right now, Volunteer Fire Companies are struggling in all aspects," Newnam said. "We need more community members to sign up to be a part of the fire service. We count on our current members to help get the equipment out, keep up with training, and help fundraise, and they are still expected to go to their jobs every day and balance family life."
Foster said the company receives operational funding from Trappe and Talbot County annually and conducts fundraisers year-round to support operations. Foster also said the company sets aside the necessary funding to maintain and acquire fire apparatus.
But the necessary funds to construct a new firehouse "far (exceed) the financial abilities of this small community," he said.
"We are a 100% volunteer fire company operating as a non-profit organization, and we are dependent on the support of our community to continue to provide the exceptional response that our community expects and deserves," Foster said.
"... Support for a new facility is absolutely necessary to allow this small-town organization to continue to provide life-saving services to the larger rural community on the Eastern Shore."
The company provides services to Trappe and surrounding communities during emergencies and life-threatening situations. It currently has a satellite county ambulance within the firehouse with a 24-hour crew for emergencies. With the construction of a new building, the firehouse will be able to provide housing quarters for a Talbot County Emergency Services Advanced Life Support unit.
Newnam said because volunteers operate the fire company, the services provided continue due to the firefighters' connection to the community. He believes that it will be through the community that the company will be able to reach its goal.
"Our members truly do it for the betterment of our community," Newnam said. "Having help with fundraising is huge for small companies like ours; without it, we have a long road ahead that we hope our building can withstand until we get to our goal."

title: Maryland man gets 8 years in crossbow killing of girlfriend
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Maryland man gets 8 years in crossbow killing of girlfriend

 February 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 790
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A man who fatally shot his live-in girlfriend with a crossbow arrow inside their Conowingo residence — maintaining that it was an accident — received an eight-year sentence on Tuesday, after a jury had convicted him of involuntary manslaughter but acquitted him of murder and assault two months earlier.Cecil County Circuit Court Administrative Judge Brenda A. Sexton imposed the eight-year sentence on 41-year-old Jeffrey Allen Lander, who also had been found guilty of reckless endangerment. At sentencing, however, that lesser charge merged into Lander's conviction for involuntary manslaughter, which carries a maximum 10-year penalty.
The victim — Judy Elizabeth Gee, 45 — was shot through the back inside the couple's residence in the 700 block of Bell Manor Road at approximately 4:40 p.m. on Jan. 14, 2024, causing heavy internal bleeding. An ambulance crew transported Gee to Lancaster General Hospital in Lancaster, Pa., where she died on an operating table at 7:13 p.m., about two and half hours later.
Sexton remarked from the bench Tuesday that Lander's "conduct was heinous," and she agreed with Assistant State's Attorney Robert Sentman's assessment that Lander exhibited a "lack of remorse or acceptance of responsibility for Gee's death," prosecutors summarized.
Sentman, who prosecuted Lander at trial, recommended a maximum 10-year sentence — exceeding state sentencing guidelines that set a penalty range of three to eight years of active incarceration for Lander. Those guidelines are based on a defendant's criminal record, the seriousness of the offense and other factors.
Lander's lawyer, Assistant Public Defender Jason Ricke, requested a sentence at the lower end of state sentencing guidelines.
Landers will serve his eight-year term in a Maryland Department of Corrections prison, and he received credit for approximately seven months that he spent in jail after his June arrest.
In November, at the conclusion of a three-day-long trial, jurors deliberated for approximately four hours before finding Lander guilty of involuntary manslaughter and reckless endangerment.
Involuntary manslaughter applies when the defendant unintentionally kills someone while acting with gross negligence, meaning the defendant should have known the risk of his or her actions. Other elements also can apply under the statute.
The jury, however, acquitted Lander of second-degree murder, first-degree assault and second-degree assault — criminal offenses that involve an intentional act, to varied degrees. Second-degree murder is punishable by up to 40 years in prison. First-degree assault and second-degree assault carry maximum sentences of 25 years and 10 years respectively.
At trial, Sentman maintained that Lander intentionally shot Gee because, during an argument moments earlier, Gee had informed Lander that she was ending their two-year relationship and that she was leaving him.
Aside from Gee, Lander was the only person present when the fatal shooting occurred — and he provided the narrative of the incident to investigators.
While police and paramedics were at the shooting scene, Gee was seated on a couch, with the arrow protruding out the entrance and exit wounds on her upper torso. She was barely conscious and was not alert. Gee wasn't capable of giving investigators her account of the incident.
The day of the fatal shooting started for Lander at about 4 p.m., with Gee jolting him awake and starting an argument with him. "She was kicking me in the knee. It was a rude awakening. I woke up angry," Lander told investigators.
Lander volunteered all of that information to investigators at the outset, after he had called 911. But in a police interview about two months later, Lander denied that he and Gee had been arguing directly before the fatal shooting.
The defense contended that Lander accidentally shot Gee with the arrow when he tripped over a cat seconds after removing his loaded crossbow from a wall rack in the living room while she was seated on a nearby couch, possibly leaning toward an end table to retrieve something.
Lander, who elected not to testify on his own behalf, told investigators that he thought the crossbow's safety was engaged and that he always stored his crossbow locked and loaded during hunting season.
In addition, Lander told investigators that he was preparing to go deer hunting that late afternoon, noting that there was about one hour of daylight left. Lander also told investigators that he liked going into the woods to decompress after confrontations with Gee.
Cecil County Sheriff's Office detectives testified that they believe Lander shot Gee in the "heat of the moment" amid the argument and that he immediately experienced regret and emotional aguish, prompting him to call 911.
Ricke, however, categorized the deadly shooting this way when addressing the jury in his opening statement: "It was a tragic accident — nothing more. It is not a murder. It is not a crime."
Police arrested and charged Lander on June 28, six months after the incident, at the conclusion of an investigation that included consulting with a crossbow expert.

title: Man pleads guilty to attempted murder in Trappe gas station shooting

 CHESAPEAKE CITY — A 63-year-old man is charged with disturbing school operation and disorderly conduct after he allegedly took numerous inappropriate photos and videos of girls playing volleyball matches inside the Bohemia Manor High School gymnasium, according to Cecil County District Court records.Investigators identified the suspect as Michael Cornell Griffin of Townsend, Del.
Maryland State Police Master Trooper Jason Proctor conducted an on-scene investigation during the incident, which occurred shortly before 8 p.m. on Thursday, and he was able to view the photographic content of the suspect's cell phone after Griffin had given verbal consent to do so, police reported.
"I reviewed the photo album and observed that it contained several photographs and videos of the junior varsity teams and varsity teams from both schools: Bohemia Manor High School and Perryville High School . . . The photographs observed in the photo album were of the buttock areas of the juvenile aged female players," Proctor summarized in his written statement of probable cause.
The investigator noted, "The uniform shorts that are worn by all the volleyball players are tight in nature; however, the photographs that were taken were zoomed in by Griffin revealing inappropriate detail, as certain curvature of the female players body parts could be clearly observed."
Court records indicate that the investigation leading to the two criminal charges against Griffin started after spectators noticed the suspect acting suspiciously in the bleachers during the volleyball game, police said. The initial complainant was a 41-year-old woman, court records show. (It is not clear if Griffin had direct ties to the volleyball competition, such as a relative who was one of the players.)
The complainants had seen the suspect "deliberately zoom in on the players' buttock areas" while he was taking digital photos with his cell phone, court records allege.
Griffin's alleged actions caused nearby parents and other spectators to ask him why he was taking pictures, creating a scene that diverted some of the spectators' attention away from the volleyball game, according to the charging document.
"This was actively causing disturbance within the stands," court records allege.
After spectators complained and pointed to the suspect, the trooper escorted Griffin from the gymnasium into the lobby, police said. Bohemia Manor Middle School Assistant Principal Stacy Rahnama was in the lobby and was present during the on-scene investigation, police added.
Proctor informed Griffin that he had been accused of taking inappropriate photos of female volleyball players, court records show. Griffin denied taking pictures of the players and started opening and closing the photo album on his phone, according to court records.
"It appeared as if he was trying to hide the photographs. Griffin appeared to be extremely nervous while speaking with me. I observed his right hand and fingers shake multiple times as he was scrolling through his phone," Proctor outlined in court records.
At that point, the trooper asked Griffin if he would be willing to show him the photos that he had taken and Griffin gave verbal consent, court records show. During that viewing of the photographic content of Griffin's cell phone, Proctor and Rahnama saw numerous inappropriate photos and videos of the female volleyball players, court records allege.
"While reviewing the photo albums, the initial complainant entered the lobby and made inquiries as to whether or not her daughter's photograph was on his phone and was making comments that she wanted the photographs deleted," according to the charging document.
Proctor then escorted Griffin out of the building and into the breezeway, where — with the suspect's consent — he and Rahnama deleted all of the questionable pictures and videos found in the phone's photo library and then from the phone's trash bin file, court records show.
"While this was taking place, a group of patrons had gathered in the lobby and were actively observing my interactions with Griffin. Another patron had to tell that group of people to remain inside and not to interfere, as they were making threats to assault Griffin due to his actions," according to the charging document, which indicates that the group obeyed and returned to the gymnasium.
After the deletion of the photos and videos, Rahnama requested that Griffin leave the school property, police said. The trooper then escorted Griffin to his 2014 Chrysler 200 that was parked in the school lot and ordered him to leave the premises, which Griffin did, police added.
At the end of his written statement of probable cause, Proctor summarized, "Griffin's direct actions of being visible while he was taking inappropriate and offensive photographs (by way of zooming in) caused direct disturbance within the stands of the sporting event which is also disruption of school activities."
Griffin was not arrested but, instead, was charged through a criminal summons that was issued on Monday, court records show. Griffin is charged with disturbing school operation, a misdemeanor that carries a maximum six-month penalty and a $2,500 fine if convicted; and disorderly conduct, which is punishable by up to 60 days in jail and a $500 fine if convicted, according to court records.
Griffin is scheduled to appear for a preliminary inquiry on Nov. 25, court records show.

 EASTON — J.R. Dobson grew up around the fire house, always knowing he wanted to be a firefighter.In his teenage years, Dobson joined the Trappe Volunteer Fire Company as a junior cadet, and by 16 he began riding the fire trucks. He fondly recalls the "everybody knew everybody" aspect of the tight-knit community.
Dobson eventually moved to Easton, beginning his journey with the Easton Volunteer Fire Department in 2003. Over time, he's served in a number of roles, including most recently, assistant chief.
Now he's taking on the department's top role for the first time. Dobson was elected the department's chief in December.
With a wife and two daughters, timing was everything for Dobson when considering the commitment to assume a role as demanding as Easton fire chief. The timing is right, he said, and he's looking forward to leading and making a difference.
"There's a lot of tradition here," Dobson said. "It's certainly the biggest department in the county. It's got probably the most going on out of all the departments in the county. I think just being here, seeing how this department operates versus a small department. It's a business. And we're all here for free, none of us get paid."
Dobson officially began as chief this month. Sonny Jones just wrapped up his third two-year term leading the department.
Dobson, who volunteers at the fire department as all the firefighters do, is a patrol and operations commander at the Talbot County Sheriff's Office. He believes his experience leading around 35 deputies across multiple divisions will translate to his duties in the fire house.
"I think that I bring a lot of management skills, leadership skills," Dobson said. "Just from my experience there, I think it helps you here."
Thus far, Dobson says the support he's received has been "overwhelming."
Past fire chiefs have reached out, and he hopes to pick up one thing from each of them to set himself up for success. For instance, Jones' ability as an incident commander is something Dobson admires.
"If there were ever a bad day anybody was having, he's who you would want there," Dobson said of Jones. "Just the way he kind of rolls through an incident scene. He's been there and done that kind of thing."
Similarly, Jones — who is remaining involved with the department — spoke highly of Dobson.
"I've known J.R. the entire time that I've been a member of the Easton fire department," Jones said. "J.R. is a first-rate guy. He's a terrific leader. He has many, many qualities which will bode well for him as the chief of the department."
Some of the ongoing projects the new fire chief has his eye on include purchasing a utility vehicle to use for Rails to Trails and woods fires, buying a new engine and updating box alarm assignments. He also wants to implement some new standard operating procedures.
Dobson said he hopes to nail down a handful of tasks for the year and keep circling back to see what progress is being made. At the top of his list is recruitment and retention of volunteers.
"I think it all starts with recruiting. I think it all starts with retention," Dobson said. "Those are things that we've done well in the past, although the last year or so we haven't gotten as many members as we would like. And sometimes we'll get members in and they don't realize the commitment."
While acknowledging the town's consistent support of the department over the years, Dobson believes Easton Fire can do better in attracting more volunteers amid struggles statewide and nationwide to fill volunteer fire departments.
"We got to get people in here," Dobson said. "We've got to get these trucks out. And I think that the way the town's growing, if we don't grow with it, then we're failing ourselves."

title: Founder of Chesapeake Bay Sight Foundation has a vision for its future
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Founder of Chesapeake Bay Sight Foundation has a vision for its future

 EASTON — Colleen Sheehan ran her accounting firm for 35 years. But this tax season was different.Sheehan, who has a rare eye disease called retinitis pigmentosa, struggled to read the tax documents of her customers. She decided to close the doors of the firm, Accounting & Management Associates, on July 1.
It's allowed her to shift focus toward a new goal: taking her nonprofit, Chesapeake Bay Sight Foundation, to new heights.
"I believe it had to happen because it made me realize this is my purpose," Sheehan said.
Diagnosed at 18 years old, Sheehan has seen every side of the degenerative disease that affects one in 4,000 people. Her mother, who went completely blind in 2000, suffered from it as well. She "never complained a day in her life," Sheehan said.
"I look at it as a blessing because if I can help one person not go through what I do every day, I've accomplished my goal," Sheehan said.
RIBBON-CUTTING
On June 14, the Chesapeake Bay Sight Foundation held a ribbon-cutting ceremony for what will soon be its new office on Beach Avenue outside of Easton. Created in 2011, the foundation aims to fund eye disease research and raise awareness about blindness.
Known for its Dining in the Dark fundraiser, in which attendees eat dinner while blindfolded, the nonprofit is looking to extend its reach, Sheehan said. With more time on her hands and the help of marketing director Breanne Tsang, Sheehan is excited for the foundation's future.
In addition to setting up and decorating the Beach Avenue office, the foundation is launching a Dine for Blind credit card, which will offer discounts at eight local restaurants for those who buy one.
In her day-to-day life, Sheehan isn't bothered by the silly mistake, whether it's wearing two different shoes or mistaking rubbing alcohol for powder. But back when the disease began to affect her, Sheehan's mindset wasn't as positive.
One day at church, Diana Mautz, the late mother of state Sen. Johnny Mautz, changed that outlook.
"One day she grabbed me and she goes, 'You've got a gift,'" Sheehan recalled. "'Your blindness is a gift. Go do something about it and help out other people.'"
"I start the foundation the next day," Sheehan said. "So she is our initiator. It was in honor of my mom and dad, but she is the woman that made me start this."
Now 13 years into existence, the foundation encourages not just eye disease research at a high level, but eye care and checkups for everyone.
"Knowing ahead of time can change everything," Sheehan said.
CLINICAL TRIAL
Chesapeake Bay Sight Foundation raises funds for the Johns Hopkins School of Medicine's Wilmer Eye Institute, which is home to the Singh Lab, run by Dr. Mandeep Singh.
Home to 17 researchers, the lab is working on finding cures to retinitis pigmentosa, macular degeneration and other eye diseases.
The Wilmer Eye Institute received more than $20 million from the National Eye Institute at the National Institutes of Health to conduct a clinical trial investigating treatment for retinitis pigmentosa.
Sheehan is hoping to participate in that clinical trial in early 2025. In September, she plans to have surgery to remove two cataracts.
No matter what the future holds, she's excited to embark on a full-fledged commitment to her nonprofit.
"I'm going blind, and I'm proud that I am," Sheehan said. "Because maybe I can make it useful and help other people."
To learn more about the Chesapeake Bay Sight Foundation, visit chesapeakebaysightfoundation.org.

title: Vietnam War vet describes life with Agent Orange
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Vietnam War vet describes life with Agent Orange

 April 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: State News

 Read News Document

 King Norris can still remember how it smelled when Agent Orange hit his nostrils while serving in Vietnam in the 1970s."Every night I went to work it was hard to breathe because of the fumes," said Norris, who worked the night shift guarding the ammo dump with the 212th MP Company in Vietnam's Long Bihn from 1970-1971. "I can't describe it, it's just unbelievable. It could knock a dragon out. I guess it was like sticking your head in a barrel of TNT."
The Chaptico resident said he was officially diagnosed with having cancer caused by exposure to Agent Orange — a chemical defoliant that U.S. troops sprayed to kill foliage and prevent the enemy from making surprise attacks — in 2015 and received nine weeks of radiation along with much-needed disability payments.
"I have friends who are Vietnam vets and one friend [known as] Lone Wolf tells of walking through the jungle and suddenly there was no jungle where they had sprayed Agent Orange, and they had to walk through that to get to where they were going," said King's brother, Joe Norris, who worked for The Enterprise and other local newspapers. "They were all affected by it. I'm grateful because King got to live a lot longer than most of them did. They've been gone, most of them, for 20, 25 years."
King, 73, also was diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2014, and a year later determined it had been caused by exposure to Agent Orange. The cancer returned with a vengeance in 2020.
"My [prostate-specific antigen] number was so high they weren't sure there was any hope for me at all," King said.
In April 2023, he went to MedStar St. Mary's Hospital in Leonardtown where a CT scan revealed a tumor in his bladder. King was put on a medication that he said cost him $15,000 a month, but his white blood count fell from 896 to 6.
Just before Christmas of last year, his back started hurting, and he was told his vertebrae was swollen and was crimping his spinal column. He was flown to Georgetown University Hospital and given 10 shots of radiation.
"King, you're dying," King said he was told by his doctor. "'Quit going to the emergency room, quit getting stents in, quit seeing doctors. There's nothing anybody can do for you. You just have to accept it. I said, 'I don't want to accept it. I want to see my little great-granddaughter grow up.'"
But through it all King was also thinking of others. He regularly brings pizzas to the nurses at the Leonardtown hospital to thank them for all they do. A card signed by many of them sits on a table next to his chair in his camper home.
"I thought, 'Well, I can't do anything about COVID,'" he said, "'but I can feed them. They appreciate the food."
When he returned to St. Mary's County following his 9-month tour in Vietnam, King became a sheetrock plasterer and was even requested by name, but in 1979 his health issues began in earnest.
"My knees started burning like crazy 24/7," King said. "It went through my body like a worm. Every joint, everything. It felt like a million spiders were crawling over my body."
"People were all like, 'It's all in his head, it's all in his head,' because there didn't seem to be anything medically wrong with him," Joe said while seated next to his brother. "I was the one who said, 'Look, you don't know what that man went through.' The stress alone of what he went through could be causing this. No matter what it is we have to stop acting like it's nothing and rally. ... It was hard."

title: Trump administration sets stage for new pandemic
author: LENA GILL
content:
Trump administration sets stage for new pandemic

 March 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LENA GILL | Section: Columns 
 
 666
 Words 

 Read News Document

 From new avian or bird flu outbreaks on the Eastern Shore to a new Ebola outbreak in Uganda, we need the World Health Organization to help mitigate pandemics and inform the world. We also need the medical detectives of the U.S. Agency for International Development to travel to an Ebola outbreak to do contact tracing to limit the exposure to the surrounding community and the world to this and other deadly diseases.None of this is possible today, as president Trump has withdrawn the U.S. from the WHO and virtually closed down the USAID.
Pulling out of the WHO creates a national security threat. For more than 75 years we have relied on it to protect us. It takes a year to withdraw, but many argue that China will probably try to step in and take it over. It is not clear if the president can withdraw from the WHO without congressional approval.
President Trump also paused the transfer of U.S. funds to the WHO. The U.S. is the largest donor, contributing about 18% of its total funding. The U.S. membership fee of $264 million for year 2024/2025 will not be paid. This violates U.S. law and will certainly be challenged in court.
In addition to the fees, there are voluntary contributions from foundations and other U.S. sources earmarked by the donors for specific purposes such as HIV and AIDS. President George W. Bush's successful PEPFAR progam dating back to 2003 has saved 26 million adults from dying of AIDS, mainly in subSaharan Africa, and 8 million babies from being born with HIV.
The funding has been frozen until March 25. This is the largest global health program dedicated to a single disease.
Polio, tuberculosis and malaria are still on the eradication list, and new viruses such as the Marburg virus, a deadly cousin of Ebola, and mpox have been declared public health emergencies in Africa. With a continuous stream of visitors to and from Africa, it seems impossible to keep any outbreak from not spreading. Viruses do not respect international borders.
Since early January, four flocks of chickens on Maryland's Eastern Shore have tested positive for the avian or bird flu virus. These outbreaks can severely affect Maryland's important poultry industry. Avian flu is often spread by wild birds, so we should not encourage such birds to feed here. Wild, infected birds have been found in Caroline County.
The bird flu in Maryland is of the H5N1 type. In California a new type has been found called the H5N9. One girl in Canada died from the bird flu and 67 farmworkers, that we know of, have been infected around the U.S.
Bird flu has been found in cows milk in California. KFF Health News has just published a report that discusses how 875 herds of cows across 16 states have tested positive for bird flu. This infection in herds of cows started about a year ago, and the Department of Agriculture has been slow to react. It announced in December 2024 its intention to test milk for bird flu nationwide. The virus dries out milk production in dairy cows and the virus now spreads between cows.
We have seen a drop of about 20% in milk production since 2023. Veterinarians are trying to save the cows. Cow hands are being infected with the H5N1 virus but not tested for the virus, partly because the tests are not readily available and partly because the cow hands may be undocumented. A few mutations of the virus could mean that it could be spread between humans. The H5N1 virus can also spread to cats. One such death was reported in Anne Arundel County.
In all of the U.S. about 100 million egg-laying birds were culled since the bird flu started in 2022. No wonder eggs now cost around $5 per dozen on the Eastern Shore or cannot be found on the shelves. Considering the bird virus in milk scare and the 20% reduction in milk produced, the price of a gallon of milk is also expected to rise.

title: Fishing trip gets disabled veterans out on the Bay

 TRAPPE — There wasn't a single cloud in the sky as disabled veterans from Pleasant Day Medical Adult Day Care took turns reeling in lines on Wednesday morning.It was a fruitful day on the water, and spirits were high. "Trust me, fishing isn't always like this," said Captain Shannon Pinkens as he threw the 10th fish in the cooler.
The event was organized by the Easton Elks 1622 Veterans Affair Committee as an opportunity for the veterans to relax and enjoy the gorgeous day.
Fishing and hunting have been shown to help combat post-traumatic stress disorder and help foster community for veterans.
A study conducted by scholars Jessie Bennet, Jennifer Piatt and Marieke Van Puymbroeck for Springer Nature found fly-fishing significantly reduced symptoms of post-traumatic stress, depression and functional impairments while increasing overall self determination and leisure satisfaction.
The United States has more veterans than any other nation in the world, and often those returning from oversees struggle to get the help they need. According to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs news, 22% of the 16.5 million veterans in 2020 were homeless and 15,000 of those individuals lived completely without shelter.
There are currently no Veteran Affairs hospitals on the Eastern Shore, but there is a clinic located in Cambridge. The closest VA hospital that provides full services is located in Baltimore.
The Easton Elks 1622 Veterans Affair Committee works to ensure these individuals, particularly disabled veterans, get the resources they need and then some.
The committee raises funds, hosts events and works with community organizations like Pleasant Day to ensure the best quality of life for veterans on the Eastern Shore, who are often far away from other resources.
Before leaving the dock Wednesday, Easton Elks 1622 Veterans Affair Chairman Michael Feehly presented Captain Pinkens with a certificate of appreciation for serving disabled veterans. Pinkens sheepishly accepted, and the crew set sail.
Once out far enough into the Bay, Pinkens and Feehly began live-baiting the lines with small shad, keeping three lines in the water at all times. As soon as there was a tug, it was on.
The rockfish were out in full force Wednesday morning. Also known as the striped bass, the rockfish is the official state fish of Maryland. Due to conservation concerns, fishers can keep one fish per person if they're between 19 and 24 inches long. Anything longer or shorter must be returned to the Bay.
Executive Director of Pleasant Day Erin Windsor aided each veteran as they reeled in the large specimen. Windsor made sure everyone got a chance to catch a fish.
The boat reached its maximum people-to-fish capacity an hour before the day was done. To wish the group farewell, a group of porpoises jumped in and out of the Bay.
"The only thing that would make this better would be a beer," said veteran Mike.

title: 'Generational trauma': Man sentenced to life in prison for 1979 murder
author: Matt Wynn mwynn@somdnews.com
content:
'Generational trauma': Man sentenced to life in prison for 1979 murder

 Author/Byline: Matt Wynn mwynn@somdnews.com | Section: News

 Andre Taylor was sentenced last week to life in prison for a murder he committed 45 years ago.Taylor, 63, was convicted of the first-degree murder of Vickie Lynn Belk by a Charles County jury on July 18. Circuit Court Judge H. James West handed down the sentence on Aug. 23.
On Aug. 28, 1979, Belk's then-boyfriend reported her missing to the Prince George's County Police Department after last seeing her on Aug. 27 at their shared place of work in Washington, D.C.
Belk had not returned to her apartment in Suitland, a release from the Charles County State Attorney's Office said.
On Aug. 29, 1979, a local teenager called 911 after noticing a body on the ground in a wooded location in the area of Metropolitan Church Road and Route 227 in Bryans Road.
Officers with the Charles County Sheriff's Office responded to the location and discovered the body of a woman with a gunshot wound to the right side of her head and undressed from the waist down, the release said.
Belk was identified the following day as the woman. The Office of the Chief Medical Examiner in Baltimore ruled her cause of death to be from the gunshot wound, the release said.
Investigators recovered, processed and maintained evidence during the initial investigation. However, the case went cold.
In the following years, several detectives worked on the case. In more recent years, Detective Sgt. John Elliott of the Charles County Sheriff's Office's Criminal Investigations Division continued the investigation and worked with various agencies to pursue leads.
As forensic technology advanced, the evidence of the murder continued to be re-examined. In 2022, the Charles sheriff's office's Forensic Science Section re-evaluated the evidence and submitted Belk's clothing for testing with newer technology. A profile was developed and entered into the Combined DNA Index System, a national DNA database.
On Nov. 1, 2022, Noelle Gehrman, the deputy director of the county sheriff's office's Forensic Science Section, was notified of a DNA match between the profiles developed from the evidence and Taylor, the release said.
While investigating Taylor's background, detectives learned that he was arrested for violent crimes that occurred in Washington, D.C. It was also discovered that Taylor lived at a residence in Bryans Road around the time of the murder.
The address was less than four miles from where Belk's body was discovered. Taylor also had connections to the area of Washington, D.C., where it is believed that Belk was abducted.
Detectives began trying to locate Taylor, but he had no known address since 2019. In collaboration with the U.S. Homeland Security Investigations, D.C. Metropolitan Police Department and the U.S. Secret Service Baltimore Field Office, detectives of the Charles sheriff's office were able to locate Taylor in Washington, D.C., where he resided.
On June 22, 2023, Taylor was arrested by the Charles County Sheriff's Office, the U.S. Marshals Service, Capital Area Regional Fugitive Task Force and members of the Metropolitan Police Department.
In an interview with detectives, Taylor admitted to actions that amounted to the rape of Belk, but he denied having any part in her murder, the release said.
At the time of the murder, Belk was 28 years old, and Taylor was 18 years old. There is no evidence that indicates that Belk and Taylor knew each other before the incident, according to the release.
During sentencing, Assistant State's Attorney John Stackhouse told the judge that the incident caused "generational trauma because it went on for 45 years. [Belk's] son grew up without a mother. Her parents had to bury their daughter. Her parents had to lay on their deathbed not knowing who killed their daughter. Her grandchildren never got a chance to meet their grandmother. Yet all throughout this case, I've never seen a family with so much grit, determination and grace."
Stackhouse added, "When you victimize someone like this and then murder them, it really doesn't get more horrific than that."
Echoing the word of Belk's son, he asked the judge to "use the power you have to get justice, and justice in this case is life [in prison]."
Before sentencing Taylor to life in prison, West said that Belk "had a presence or spirit that has endured in ways that I've honestly never seen before," furthering that the "victim leaves a tremendous legacy, and the family carries on a tremendous legacy."
The judge also stated that "the crime is a horrific loss of a life — the violence was extreme. The amount of fear and terror that preceded the violence doesn't exist in most cases. [The incident was] so heinous, I can't think of a lesser sentence that would be appropriate."

title: Limits on how much a drug should cost
author: Susan Estrich
content:
Limits on how much a drug should cost

 September 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Susan Estrich | Page: A6 | Section: News 
 
 602
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The U.S. government last week released the list of the 10 medications that will be the first to be the subject of the new price negotiations under the Medicare reform bill, and my arthritis drug, Enbrel, made the list.To make the cut, you either had to be taken by millions of people, like Eliquis, or cost a fortune. Enbrel costs a fortune.I'm one of 47,000 Medicare recipients lucky enough to receive a drug that my old rheumatologist, who originally prescribed it for me, described as a miracle.When he was a young doctor, he told me, his waiting room of patients with rheumatoid arthritis was full of crippled people. With the advent of "biologic" drugs like Enbrel, the crutches and wheelchairs are gone. I count myself very lucky to be mostly symptom-free, which, with RA, is saying a lot. As I say, I'm lucky and blessed. And well-insured.And able to cover the out-ofpocket costs. Which are also substantial.This is the hard part of medical miracles.One month, when I was switching insurance companies, I ran out of Enbrel. I made the mistake of thinking I could actually pay for my weekly shot out-of-pocket if I couldn't get the insurance situation straightened out. "How much would it be?" I naively asked the pharmacist. Enbrel is a SureClick pen; it comes in a pack of four. That would be $1,700 for one pen and $7,000 for the pack.Excuse me? Who can afford that?I managed to get a sample from the doctor's office to tide me over and never asked again. Every month when the specialty pharmacy calls me to renew my Medicare prescription, they confirm my $350 co-pay and I don't so much as murmur a word of complaint, because what can I say? The drug saves my life. But I'm lucky I can afford it. That's why Enbrel belongs on the list.Medicines like Enbrel cost billions to develop, and it is only fair that those costs be recouped. But there are limits, and there is no reason that the market should be foreclosed from working freely when it comes to the prices for these prescription drugs. Enbrel costs too much, but there is nothing that I, one consumer, can do about it. We need to stand together, which is to say, we need government to stand up for us and negotiate for us and give voice to our needs.What is stunning about these negotiations is that it took an act of Congress to authorize the government to use the power of the people on behalf of the people to negotiate fair drug prices.The power of the pharmaceutical industry was so great, so much greater than the power of the American people, that it was literally the law of the land that Medicare could not use its bargaining power on behalf of the American taxpayer.When the bill allowing price negotiation passed last year, the Congressional Budget Office predicted the program would save Medicare more than $100 billion during the next 10 years.Just stop and consider that for a moment: the biggest purchaser of health services unable to use its bargaining power, on behalf of you and I, leaving the industry's power to set prices unchecked. And yet this is precisely what government is for, precisely what government is meant to do, to stand up for and give voice to we the people. The pharmaceutical industry continues to fight against negotiations in the courts. "Today is the start of a new deal for patients where Big Pharma doesn't just get a blank check at your expense and the expense of the American people," President Joe Biden said in announcing the list.It's about time.COPYRIGHT 2023 CREATORS.COM

 EASTON — An Easton man received an 18-year sentence on Thursday for third-degree sex offense against his then-3-year-old daughter, among other offenses.Kevin Manning, 34, appeared in court to hear his fate after entering a guilty plea for the felony sex offense and nine other counts, including witness intimidation, electronic communication harassment and violation of a protective order. Those nine counts were levied for actions he took against his daughter's mother after the Sept. 2024 assault of the daughter.
Talbot County Circuit Court Judge Phil Cronan handed down the 18-year sentence — a term exceeding the recommended five- to 13-year range — for what he called a "vicious and heinous" crime.
Before Cronan delivered the sentence, Deputy State's Attorney Chelsea Endzel asked the court for a 30-year sentence.
Endzel cited Manning's past sex assault convictions: a fourth-degree sex offense in Anne Arundel County in 2016 and second-degree rape in Talbot County in 2022 stemming from a 2009 incident involving Manning and an underage female living with him at the time.
The rape conviction was dismissed in 2023 after it was determined that the judge who postponed Manning's trial date was not designated to do so.
Endzel argued for the extended sentence, in part, due to Manning's "repeated harassment" of the child's mother, Emily Hiester, beginning last September. Endzel wrote in a memo to the court that Manning contacted Hiester nearly 200 times through emails and phone calls, violating a protective order.
Endzel read a written impact statement from Hiester, in which the mother said she couldn't bear to be in a courtroom with Manning. Hiester wrote that she has secluded herself from others and that she "can see the pain" in her daughter's eyes.
"I can't see others the same when someone I thought I knew I could trust did something so horrible," a portion of the statement read.
Hiester asked for Manning's sentence to be "as much time as the court will allow."
Endzel also argued that an open District Court case in which Manning is accused of assaulting an inmate at the Talbot County Detention Center factors into the danger he poses to society. The alleged assault occurred May 24.
"The question is not whether he will reoffend, but when," Endzel said.
Manning's defense attorney, Holly Brownley of the public defender's office, asked Cronan to deliver a sentence within the pre-sentence recommendations.
Manning "had some serious traumas in his young life," such as the murder of his mother and being exposed to drug and substance abuse, Brownley said.
The 34-year-old defendant, in an orange suit, handcuffs and wide black glasses, spoke for a few minutes at the hearing Thursday. He said he wants to go to a maximum-security prison, Patuxent Institution in Jessup, to receive treatment.
Manning acknowledged his daughter was the victim and said what occurred was an accident. He disagreed with Endzel's claims that he has shown no remorse.
"To ostracize me from society, I don't believe's appropriate," Manning said, noting that since 2019, he doesn't feel he's been a "trouble or menace" to society.
Cronan disagreed with that assessment.
The judge said Manning's behavior has escalated the last 15 years. The dismissed rape conviction is "certainly something ... in this court's mind," Cronan said. He added that the sex offense conviction and a related burglary crime from 2016 as well as the pending assault case from two months ago played a role.
"That doesn't sound to me that you haven't been any trouble," Cronan told Manning. "Quite the opposite."
The judge said the facts of the case were clear: Manning assaulted his daughter and "manipulated the mother of your child" to try to get her to lie in court for him.
Cronan said the daughter "should have the comfort" to be with her father without such a thing happening.
In addition to the 18 years, Manning is ordered to be on probation for five years after his release, make no contact with Hiester or the daughter and not visit their residences, schools, places of employment or daycares. He will register as a Tier III sex offender.

title: Drivers need patience on roadways

 As a senior driver of 70 years driving experience I have finally reached my frustration point in what I (correctly or incorrectly) perceive as unwarranted impatience, if not absolute rudeness and discourtesy, on the part of drivers in Talbot County.I am a competent, not perfect, operator of a motor vehicle, and I do not understand the needs of many other drivers, younger ones in particular, to honk their horns, pass on the right side, ride your bumper or even pass on a double line when I take a needed extra second or two to double check when I am making a turn, entering an intersection, leaving a stop light, or driving at what I consider a safe 40 mph on the narrow, winding and crowned blacktop roads here, many of which have no shoulders only ditches.
You drivers who are speeding and tailgating in our county — and you, in my experience are many —will get where you are going without putting me or yourselves in danger. An absolutely unneeded honking horn is startling and rather than achieving its likely objective of hurrying me along and making me drive in the manner in which you think I should be driving actually slows me down when I look once more to reassess the situation around me before I move away from that light or stop sign or turn against traffic.
You will be senior drivers someday yourself, and you will understand certain facts — namely your reaction time slows a touch, your hearing and vision, though adequate for the task, are not what they used to be and your trust in your own cognition in discerning what is happening around you is quite naturally slightly diminished.
Talbot County and the town of Easton today present challenging driving conditions. The sheer volume of traffic, the narrow streets in town with double parking, and the plethora of large sized pickups and SUVs plying streets and roadways here that were not designed for these types of vehicles are factors, as well as the presence of some dangerous intersections lacking traffic controls — one of these is one I use daily, the intersection of the Parkway and Tristan Drive. I do not need an accident at my age, whether my fault or not. This is a major reason I (and many others of my age) need that extra moment of time to cope safely and competently with the driving situations already mentioned. title: Health department recommends making condoms available at local high school

content:
Health department recommends making condoms available at local high school

 January 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LAURA TAYMAN | Section: News

 Last month, Kent County Board of Education members were provided stark facts about the rise in sexually transmitted diseases (STD) in the community, the state, and the country at its recent monthly meeting.Ashley Minietta, communicable disease and family planning contact for the Kent County Department of Health, made a presentation to the board before the holiday break, saying the solution to reversing the trend is "to provide ground support, monitor trends, and turn data into action."
"While 20% of Marylanders have an STD, almost half of the cases are ages 15-24," Minietta said, citing the 2020 U.S. census map — putting Maryland in the South region of the country, "It's one of the highest rates in the region."
Minietta said the barriers to effectively preventing both STDs and teenage pregnancies in Kent County are lack of education, the cost of birth control, parental resistance to alternatives, lack of public transportation, the geographic barriers of the rural area and lack of health care options.
Teen pregnancy rates are down, Minietta said, because parents have been proactive with putting teenage daughters on birth control. But pills and IUDs do not allow the prevention of STDs that can lead to long-term health consequences.
"Research in 2020 shows only 9% of sexually active high school students used a condom," Minetta said. "That has only increased."
Minetta shared various ways local school systems are providing a condom availability program to meet the needs of their high school students, including those in Queen Anne's, Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot and Wicomico counties, and counties on the western shore.
While some have availability through the school's nurse's office, others provide a "brown bag" approach, where students can pick up a paper bag on an anonymous basis.
Board member Aretha Dorsey said that as a parent she was concerned that a program like that would encourage secrets among parents and their children.
"I feel like parents' rights are being taken away," Dorsey said. "I believe that kids might form a lack of respect for their parents and think they can do things their own way."
Board member Francois Sullivan said Kent County and its rural location is a valid argument for such a program.
"There is a difference between a nurse providing condoms and a cashier."
When asked to share her opinion, student board member Madison Messick said she couldn't even remember her sex education class.
"I think this is really important," she said. "There is a stigma. We can't go to Walgreens because we know the cashier. I know kids that would definitely benefit from this."
Vienna Walker, supervisor of student services for the Board, said she recommended the board adopt a policy where Kent County students can meet with a high school nurse and ask for information and guidance.
Superintendent Karen Couch said she had been asked by parents how students could be opted out of a program if they don't approve. Walker said she would need to check with the state's Department of Education to see how that could be handled.
"Some students have much more open communication with school nurses than their parents," Walker said. "Their office is much less threatening to students who then become comfortable enough to come back if they are not feeling great."
That is Walker's goal. She recommended the board consider approving a program that requires students to visit nurses who can provide education and guidance on condom use.
"Nurses also encourage students to be open and honest with their parents," Walker said.
Messick agreed.
"Students will participate not because kids don't trust their parents," she said. "The program encourages conversations between parents and their children. It's like therapy where they can't tell parents what their child is talking about. This actually helps to form a better relationship between students and parents."
School Board President Joe Goetz said he would like for Walker to get information from other districts on how they manage parent objections.
"I think real life examples would help," Goetz said.

 An earthquake shook Maryland Friday morning, with residents across the region reporting rumbling in an area where people are unaccustomed to feeling the ground move.The U.S. Geological Survey reported a quake at 10:23 a.m. with a preliminary magnitude of 4.8, centered near Lebanon, N.J., or about 45 miles west of New York City and 50 miles north of Philadelphia. USGS figures indicated that the quake might have been felt by more than 42 million people.
Across social media, users from Crumpton, Centreville, Worton, Ridgely, Wye Mills and Easton felt the quake. In Chester, one woman reported small vibration, less than 10 seconds. Melonie Mattison of Kent Island said she was sitting at here dining table when the chair wobbled.
For most though, unless they were sitting still, it was an easy to miss experience here on the Shore. As Justin Davis quipped, "I felt more trembles when a tractor trailer passes by."
The shaking stirred memories of the Aug. 23, 2011, earthquake that jolted tens of millions of people from Georgia to Canada. Registering magnitude 5.8, it was the strongest quake to hit the East Coast since World War II. The epicenter was in Virginia.
In Newark, Delaware, Friday morning, dozens of readers told the Newark Post they felt the shaking.
"My house shook," one person said. Another reported "a rumble and a strange noise." On Old Paper Mill Road, a resident said her walls and floors were shaking.
Ann Marie Drozdick was in her apartment at Regency Square Apartments near Fairfield when the earthquake struck.
"The whole place was shaking," Drozdick said. "It was shaking and shivering. The dishes and everything were shaking."
At first she wasn't sure what was happening.
"It didn't last too long, 30 seconds, and then it stopped," she said. "I went out in the hallway and the neighbor said it's an earthquake."
Amtrak said it was inspecting its tracks Friday and had speed restrictions in place throughout the busy Northeast Corridor. New Jersey Transit posted on X that its train system was subject to delays caused by bridge inspections. The Philadelphia area's PATCO rail line suspended service out of what it said was "an abundance of caution."
Earthquakes are less common on this side of the U.S. because the East Coast does not lie on a boundary of tectonic plates. But East Coast quakes can still pack a punch — its rocks are better at spreading earthquake energy across far distances.
"If we had the same magnitude quake in California, it probably wouldn't be felt nearly as far away," said U.S.G.S. geophysicist Paul Caruso.

The commissioners' concerns largely dealt with who would manage and staff the new facility, as well as how authority over the facility would be divided among the three participating counties.
"All the employees would be Queen Anne's county employees," Caroline County Commission President Travis Breeding said. "The Warden, and all the way through the chain of command would be Queen Anne's workers, and honestly, I'm really struggling with the investment."
The potential detention center would be located at the former Eastern Pre-Release Unit site at 700 Flat Iron Square Road near Church Hill.
The center aims to address the growing need for modern and efficient detention facilities in the region, where counties are struggling to finance renovations or replacements of their aging detention facilities.
Last year, Caroline County sent a letter expressing interest in participating in the project. But Tuesday, the commissioners made it clear that they were not quite ready to sign on.
Caroline County Commissioners proposed a regional authority to manage the detention center, which is not mentioned in the drafter agreement.
"The item that we are still trying to hammer out is the agreement, we were under the impression that we were going to form a regional authority to manage the detention center," County Administrator Katheleen Freeman said.
The majority of the authority over the center will be in Queen Anne's County hands, according to the draft. All decisions and disagreement must go through Queen Anne's County Commissioners, and if they may have a disagreement it will be mediated.
The Caroline County commissioners also expressed concerns about the autonomy and authority of the the new facility's warden. According to the draft agreement, "The Board shall appoint a Warden to operate the Facility with the consent of the County Commissioners of Queen Anne's County."
The draft agreement also states that "The Warden's contract shall not be terminated without the Board's consent"
The commissioners voiced that they believed under the draft that Queens Anne's county could decide after a certain amount of time to remove Caroline or Kent county from agreement, regardless of the amount of money that was put up. To remove one or both of the other counties from the agreement, according to the draft, Queen Anne's County must give the other county a two-year notice to take all their prisoners and house them somewhere else.
The commissioners said they understood Queen Anne's County's decision to conduct the draft agreement this way, but they requested further negotiation and discussion to establish a partnering jurisdiction.
