 EASTON — Medical student Tahreem Riaz said her interest in rural healthcare was established due to the rural community she grew up in Punjab, Pakistan.Riaz is one of six students who has been chosen for the University of Maryland School of Medicine's new rural health initiative to address the physician shortage on the Eastern Shore.
Rural areas in Maryland have notoriously been medically underserved, according to the federal Health Resource and Services Administration. Students like Riaz are taking initiative to address these disparities and help close the medical disparity through the Rural Health Equity and Access Longitudinal Elective.
The students will be provided didactic and mentoring sessions as well as research and clinical experiences on the Eastern Shore.
Leah Millstein, the program director and associate professor of medicine, said there's a real challenge for the population of the Eastern Shore in finding and accessing exemplary healthcare.
"There's a shortage in primary care doctors as well as specialties, and we often have students who are interested in rural medical care in their futures, but their exposure to it during medical school is limited," Millstein said. "So this program seeks to fill those gaps, to really give the students an in depth exposure to rural health care, and give them the building blocks that allow them to feel like they'll be successful serving as physicians in those communities when they're done with their training."
Riaz said her initial circumstances in Punjab made her realize the importance of one-to-one connection with patients and their medical providers.
"I personally faced the challenges of not discussing quality healthcare due (to a) shortage of physicians," Riaz said. "Individuals of my village have to go to far off places to get necessary healthcare."
The program is designed to train and place incoming medical students in Eastern Shore healthcare practices. About $1.4 million has been secured in state funding and from the University of Maryland, Baltimore; University of Maryland Eastern Shore; the Rural Maryland Council and many donors.
Millstein said three of the six students accepted into the program were awarded full-tuition scholarships with a commitment to working on the Eastern Shore for four years after completing residency training. The long-term goal is to support 10 students interested in rural health in this elective program each year.
Ken Kozel, president and CEO of University of Maryland Shore Regional Health, said this program will help draw new providers to the Eastern Shore.
"Strengthening our provider workforce is a top priority at UM SRH, and programs like R-HEALE will help us attract providers who want to practice in rural communities," Kozel said. "We greatly appreciate our partnership with the School of Medicine toward enhancing access across the Shore."
For Riaz, she is happy for the opportunity to focus on improving rural areas and assisting caring for the people in rural areas.
"With this program, I'll be able to be involved in research projects that are deeply focused on improving population and community health, and also to deeply understand the social, economic or cultural factors that are rooted in the disparities of such communities," she said. "I think this comprehensive training through our field will allow me to deliver more compassionate and patient centered care in the future."

 ANNAPOLIS — Children as young as 10 could potentially go to court for auto thefts and handgun violations, under one proposal key Democratic lawmakers detailed on Wednesday and plan to push for in the legislature in coming weeks.The lawmakers propose giving Juvenile Services officers the option to route a young person's case to court if the child is 10 to 13 years of age and accused of these or other crimes — adding them to the list of serious offenses that already can land a young person before a judge.
The proposals are meant to promote collaboration and make the system work more smoothly, Democratic officials said, but youth advocates worry that they will lead to higher incarceration rates, especially of youth of color.
"Right now, juvenile offenders and the services and accountability they need are separated by an abundance of confusion," said House Speaker Adrienne Jones, D-Baltimore County. "Egos, political agendas and arguments over process have filled the gaps."
There must be "accountability for adults in the system, who are charged with administering the system," said Senate President Bill Ferguson, D-Baltimore City. "We must ensure that all parts are working to their highest potential."
Jones and Ferguson joined Democratic Gov. Wes Moore on Wednesday for a public announcement of the proposals, alongside the lawmakers who crafted them.
The raft of changes, if enacted, would toughen a reform law the state legislature passed in 2022. Among other things, that reform barred police from charging young people under 13 except when they are accused of the most serious crimes.
The newly unveiled legislative package would expand that list of serious crimes and lengthen the maximum probation period that can be ordered by a judge. It would also expand the reporting responsibilities of a state agency charged with oversight of the youth justice system.
The announcement on Wednesday gave shape to Democrats' response to pleas for accountability amid spikes in certain youth offenses in recent years. While youth violent crime arrests fell 16.5% overall between fiscal years 2020 and 2023, according to a Juvenile Services report last year, carjackings increased by 85.4% and handgun violations rose almost 220%.
After weeks of talks with law enforcement and advocates, the set of proposals represents a general agreement among Democrats, who control both chambers of the legislature and also hold the governor's office.
But advocates in the Maryland Youth Justice Coalition predicted in a written statement that the "legislation introduced today will see thousands more kids incarcerated every year, particularly Black and brown children, and (exacerbate) the already serious racial disparities in Maryland's juvenile justice system."
As the minority party, Republicans have said in recent months that the reform law leaves Marylanders less safe and also prevents young people from getting the services they need. GOP lawmakers in Annapolis have their own ideas for change, including a measure that would prohibit young people who have committed sexual offenses from attending school in person.
But one key Republican on Wednesday said the Democrats' plan shows they are taking "first steps" in addressing flaws in the youth justice system. House Minority Leader Jason Buckel, R-Allegany, said he appreciates that Moore has put his weight behind the issue of youth crime.
"For him to be able to step in and say, 'Hey, I'm a Democrat. I'm from Baltimore City, but I'm going to step up and say too much is too much and this is a reasonable way to deal with this' — it's incredibly helpful," Buckel said.
Buckel said he also hopes Moore will be able to persuade fellow Democrats to consider other tough ideas, too.

Embracing the calm: New yoga studio coming to Shore

 Big things are happening at 932 Washington Avenue, Suite G in Chestertown. The soon-to-be new yoga studio, Slack Tide Yoga, is starting to take shape. Owner, Adriane Watson, excitedly shared construction on the interior began in February.With only minor modifications required — updating signage, flooring, paint, bathroom finishes, lighting and in-studio heat — Watson is using Second Wind Contracting to furnish the interior improvements. While that happens, she said, "I get to source the fun parts — scents, art, furniture and decor, all thoughtfully curated to create a serene environment that nods to the nearby waterways and landscapes. As you pass by in the coming weeks, you'll notice a bright green banner hanging in front of the location."
Slack Tide Yoga studio aims at helping each person, no matter their fitness level or needs.
Watson explains, "My highest priority is to create an environment where my members feel comfortable, above all else. Prospective students can expect a welcoming, judgment and stigma-free atmosphere. I believe in cultivating spaces that make practicing yoga approachable, attainable and welcoming for everyone — regardless of experience, body type, age, etc. My goal is to help students create embodied experiences that create opportunities for them to feel present and connected to themselves in a world that so frequently pressures us to disassociate, perform and hustle."
Watson, is well-known locally for teaching at TwoTen (Chestertown), Kent County YMCA and Fit Flock (Chestertown), and Soul Society Yoga (Kent Island). She is a 200-hour registered yoga teacher with 15 years of personal yoga practice. Watson explained, "I moved to Church Hill from Centreville in 2020, and quickly realized that commuting to Kent Island or Middletown for personal practice is not convenient, given the distance.
Chestertown's existing boutique wellness industry combined with robust attendance in my Chestertown classes and feedback from my students reinforced my intuition that people here would respond positively to a dedicated yoga studio that offered a consistent schedule of offerings. Aside from affording an excellent opportunity to develop physical wellness, a yoga studio can also foster a sense of community and serve as a safe haven wherein students can find respite from the rigorous demands of daily life — something I believe we all need. Sometimes, the difference between feeling well versus feeling unwell is simply having somewhere to go."
The name 'Slack Tide' has a special meaning that sets the tone for the yoga studio. Her website explains. "There's a moment sailors call slack tide, when the tide is neither coming in nor going out, but perfectly still. It's a moment frozen in time. When all is calm and peaceful. Much like the serene interval between tidal movements, yoga offers a space for stillness, where the ceaseless waves of daily challenges momentarily recede. Embracing the calm within, practitioners find themselves in a state of mental and physical equilibrium. Just as the slack tide is a pause before the next surge, yoga provides a pause in the rhythm of life, inviting practitioners to discover inner peace, balance, and strength before navigating the dynamic waters beyond the mat."
What can the public look forward to? Watson said, "While the class schedule is not yet finalized, I will offer a well-rounded schedule of classes, including vinyasa (otherwise known as flow — dynamic sequences with movement linked to breath), yin (a passive, mostly floor-based practice with principles of Traditional Chinese Medicine. Postures are held for 5-7 minutes with the goal of targeting deep connective tissues), gentle/slow flow (gradual progression between postures, incorporating more time for breathwork and meditation) and classes designed specifically for beginners that teach the foundational movements. In the future, I plan to offer chair yoga and a strength and balance class, both of which would be appropriate for beginners or anyone with physical limitations. I am exploring options to offer heated classes as well.
As an instructor, Watson likes to emphasize functional movement, and offers sequences that explore mobility while building strength at the end range of motion. "My classes always have great playlists, a light mood and a long savasana," she said. Additionally, they'll offer special workshops on posture and alignment, along with events like sound baths and collaborations with other wellness providers (think yoga + acupuncture, essential oils, etc). Watson said she welcomes anyone who is curious, or even hesitant, about beginning a yoga practice to stop by and have a chat so they can find the right class for them. She'll also offer private instruction for students who may want more individualized attention.
Although the opening date is not set yet, Slack Tide Yoga studio is predicted to open in early spring 2024. Stay tuned for more information on opening day and an open house by following the studio on Facebook at Slack Tide Yoga Studio, Instagram at @slacktideyoga studio or sign up for email updates at www.slacktideyoga.com.

 GRASONVILLE — Saturday evening, Nov. 16, Talisman Therapeutic Riding hosted its second annual Horseshoe Heroes Awards Banquet at the Hyatt Place hotel, located at Kent Narrows.Event Chair and emcee Audrey Scott welcomed those in attendance, explaining the purpose of the banquet was to recognize those in the community who have supported the mission of Talisman Therapeutic Riding, an organization providing horse therapy to disabled military veterans, children, and other individuals.
Following dinner, guest speaker U.S. Coast Guard Captain Carrie Wolfe spoke briefly, talking about related services the Coast Guard provides to members of the military, particularly those struggling with mental health issues. She stated, "We not only use horses for therapy treatments, but other animals such as dogs and others, to help members of the military improve their quality of life."
Scott was joined by TTR Chair Diana Saquella and Queen Anne's County Commissioner Jim Moran during the presentations. Moran read a biography of each honoree.
Talisman Therapeutic Riding has been in existence for more that a decade. Executive Director Noelle Douglas said, "This banquet is held to recognize our volunteers and members of the community who go above and beyond to help Talisman."
The Talisman farm and facility is located at 172 Blue Ribbon Lane in Grasonville. For more information, visit talismantherapeuticriding.org or call 443-239-9400.
The Honorees
Business of the Year — The McMahon Consulting Group, which fulfilled the terms of an $80,000 AmeriCorps planning grant.Volunteer of the Year — Beth Cole has been a part of the Talisman family since 2014 as a PATH certified instructor, committed to two days a week helping countless students become more independent.Neighbor of the Year — Sara and Rami Essaid, described as "lifelong champions of animal welfare," they share the (Talisman) Blue Ribbon address with a magnificent group of horses, goats, cows, dogs, cats and a pig.Philanthropist of the Year — Cal Gray Jr. reduced Talisman's mortgage by 70% in the past year.
